provenance: With Jacques Petithory, Paris, where purchased by the present owner in 1969 | Private Collection, France | | This finely executed drawing could possibly be considered a study for Jean-Baptiste Wicar's La Résurrection du fils de la veuve de Naïm, now at the Palais des Beaux-Arts de Lille (P667), a subject drawn from the Gospel of Luke (7:11-17). provenance: Private collection, France | | The present lot is a rediscovered painting by Michel Corneille the Younger (1642–1708) which has remained in the same French family for decades. | Corneille was one of the leading painters of the French classical tradition and a prominent figure in the Académie Royale de Peinture et de Sculpture. Trained in the French classical manner, he was also influenced by the Italianate style of the Carracci and was celebrated for his allegorical and decorative works, many executed to royal commissions, most notably at the Palace of Versailles. | | This painting represents a second version of Corneille's celebrated Aspasie au milieu des philosophes de la Grèce, commissioned by Louis XIV in 1672 for the eastern vault of the Queen's Salon des Nobles at the Palace of Versailles (INV 3339 BIS F). While the Versailles painting presents a harmonious arrangement of figures in a monumental format, the present version introduces subtle variations in composition and iconography, reflecting the artist's exploration of alternative spatial and narrative solutions. These differences reveal Corneille's methodical approach to allegorical painting and his concern with clarity, balance, and expressive nuance. | | Two preparatory drawings by the artist for the present work, in the Staedel Museum, Frankfurt (inv. 1060 Z) and the Weimar Museum (inv. KK 8727) reveal his compositional planning and careful study of figural interactions.

provenance: Acquired by the parents of the present owner | Thence by descent | Private collection, France | | | The great marine painter Ivan Konstantinovich Aivazovsky, widely regarded as the pre-eminent master of seascapes, inspired countless students and followers during his lifetime. In 1865, in his native city of Feodosia in Crimea, he founded an art workshop that soon evolved into a fully-fledged school of painting. Unlike the rigid academic training prevalent in the Russian Empire at the time, Aivazovsky's school offered a distinctly different approach, one that placed emphasis on the direct observation of nature. | | At the heart of Aivazovsky's teaching philosophy was the belief that true artistry lies not in the mechanical reproduction of reality, but in the emotional and perceptual interpretation of it. He urged his students to study nature in all its moods - its light, movement and rhythm, and to internalise these impressions before expressing them on canvas. His method encouraged young painters to paint not merely what they saw, but what they felt. | | The School of Aivazovsky became a cradle of marine art in the region and attracted aspiring painters from across the world. Under the master's guidance, they developed a deep sensitivity to the seascape and learned to convey the boundless energy of the sea with both technical skill and emotional resonance. The school laid the groundwork for an entire generation of marine artists, and its influence extended well beyond Crimea. | | The present work, attributed to the School of Aivazovsky, bears all the hallmarks of the master's genius. The subject matter, the treatment of colour and light, and the beloved Crimean landscape - all these elements are quintessentially Aivazovskian. The painting vividly expresses the beauty of nature and the radiant play of light, while simultaneously conveying the formidable power of the sea and its dominance over the frailty of man. | | The sea in this painting is alive - it breathes, it moves. The artist has rendered it with remarkable mastery, using a wide range of blues: from the nearly black, indigo depths to the transparent turquoise that laps at the shore. The play of light is particularly virtuosic. In the background, the sea appears dark and threatening, suggesting danger or loss, while the foreground is illuminated by soft highlights, a luminous glimmer that evokes hope, as though a ray of salvation has found a lone survivor of a shipwreck. | | The composition is carefully structured to emphasise the vastness and majesty of nature. The smallness of man is not just a motif but a philosophy. In this, the painting captures a romantic ideal that was central to Aivazovsky's vision: the sea as both muse and master, eternally powerful and ineffably beautiful. artwork_title: La villa de Tiberius à Capri
provenance: Private collection, Italy |  | A prominent figure of the Düsseldorf School, Achenbach embarked on his initial Italian journey in 1845, which profoundly influenced his artistic direction. He later returned in 1850, visiting Rome and the Campagna, and again in 1857, exploring Naples and Capri. These experiences deepened his engagement with Mediterranean landscapes and classical antiquities. His 1871 sojourn included Castellammare di Stabia, Amalfi, Capri, and Ischia, further enriching his oeuvre.
